claim: Calcium is a universal second messenger present in all eukaryotic cells.
source: Calcium is a universal second messenger present in all eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about calcium's role in cellular signaling.

claim: The mobilization and storage of Ca2+ ions drives a number of signaling-related processes, stress–responses, or metabolic changes, all of which are relevant for the development of immune cells and their adaption to pathogens.
source: The mobilization and storage of Ca2+ ions drives a number of signaling-related processes, stress–responses, or metabolic changes, all of which are relevant for the development of immune cells and their adaption to pathogens.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific consensus about calcium's role in immune cell function.

claim: The YellowCaB mouse expresses the genetically encoded calcium indicator TN-XXL in B lymphocytes.
source: Here, we introduce the Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET)-reporter mouse YellowCaB expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator TN-XXL in B lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing TN-XXL expression in B cells.

claim: Calcium-induced conformation change of TN-XXL results in FRET-donor quenching measurable by two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging.
source: Calcium-induced conformation change of TN-XXL results in FRET-donor quenching measurable by two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental methodology and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Absolute cytoplasmic calcium concentrations in activated B cells during affinity maturation in vivo can be extracted using a novel numerical analysis.
source: For the first time, using our novel numerical analysis, we extract absolute cytoplasmic calcium concentrations in activated B cells during affinity maturation in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the FLIM data and phasor analysis methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: Calcium in activated B cells is highly dynamic.
source: We show that calcium in activated B cells is highly dynamic and that activation introduces a persistent calcium heterogeneity to the lineage.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved imaging data showing fluctuating calcium concentrations.

claim: Activation introduces a persistent calcium heterogeneity to the B cell lineage.
source: We show that calcium in activated B cells is highly dynamic and that activation introduces a persistent calcium heterogeneity to the lineage.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of calcium concentrations across different B cell subsets.

claim: An elevation of cytoplasmic calcium from external space is mostly mediated through ligand binding to surface receptors (Baba et al., 2014).
source: An elevation of cytoplasmic calcium from external space is mostly mediated through ligand binding to surface receptors (Baba et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baba et al., 2014.

claim: In the germinal center, ligand density in the form of native antigen, stimuli for toll-like receptors, or chemokine receptors is high.
source: Especially in the germinal center (GC), where B cells fine-tune their B cell receptor (BCR) in order to become positively selected by T cells, ligand density in the form of native antigen (AG), stimuli for toll-like receptors (TLR), or chemokine receptors, is high.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the germinal center microenvironment.

claim: Selected B cells that leave the GCs fuel the pool of memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells.
source: Selected B cells that leave the GCs fuel the pool of memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about B cell differentiation pathways.

claim: Long-lived plasma cells produce high-affinity antibodies granting up to lifelong protection against threats such as infectious diseases.
source: These cells produce high-affinity antibodies granting up to lifelong protection against threats such as infectious diseases, but also can account for the persistence of an autoimmune phenotype, when selection within the GC is impaired (Berek et al., 1991; da Silva et al., 1998; Hiepe et al., 2011; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Long-lived plasma cells can account for the persistence of an autoimmune phenotype when selection within the GC is impaired.
source: These cells produce high-affinity antibodies granting up to lifelong protection against threats such as infectious diseases, but also can account for the persistence of an autoimmune phenotype, when selection within the GC is impaired (Berek et al., 1991; da Silva et al., 1998; Hiepe et al., 2011; Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: B cell activation by AG uptake through the BCR promotes calcium influx into B cells (Tolar et al., 2009).
source: B cell activation by AG uptake through the BCR promotes calcium influx into B cells (Tolar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tolar et al., 2009.

claim: Calcium mobilization switches on effector proteins and transcription factors like nuclear factor kappa B, nuclear factor of activated T cells, or myelocytomatosis oncogene cellular homolog.
source: Calcium mobilization eventually switches on effector proteins and transcription factors like nuclear factor kappa B, nuclear factor of activated T cells, or myelocytomatosis oncogene cellular homolog, thereby inducing differentiation events and remodeling of metabolic requirements (Crabtree and Olson, 2002; Jellusova, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Saijo et al., 2002; Su et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Calcium mobilization induces differentiation events and remodeling of metabolic requirements.
source: Calcium mobilization eventually switches on effector proteins and transcription factors like nuclear factor kappa B, nuclear factor of activated T cells, or myelocytomatosis oncogene cellular homolog, thereby inducing differentiation events and remodeling of metabolic requirements (Crabtree and Olson, 2002; Jellusova, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Saijo et al., 2002; Su et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: B cells receive additional, costimulatory signals dependent on the amount of AG taken up and the quality of MHCII-mediated presentation to T follicular helper cells (Gitlin et al., 2015).
source: Dependent on the amount of AG taken up and the quality of major histocompatibility complex II (MHCII)-mediated presentation to T follicular helper cells, B cells receive additional, costimulatory signals (Gitlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gitlin et al., 2015.

claim: Costimulatory signals have to occur within a limited period of time after initial BCR activation, with the limit set by a calcium threshold leading to mitochondrial dysfunction (Akkaya et al., 2018).
source: Interestingly, recent studies propose that costimulatory signals have to occur within a limited period of time after initial BCR activation and that the limit is set by a calcium threshold, eventually leading to mitochondrial dysfunction (Akkaya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Akkaya et al., 2018.

claim: Absolute calcium measurements in B cells have not yet been performed in vivo, partly because of the lack of internal concentration standards.
source: In contrast to qualitative description, absolute calcium measurements in B cells have not yet been performed in vivo, partly because of the lack of internal concentration standards.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: Two-fluorophore genetically encoded calcium indicators relying on FRET can take on a calcium-saturated (quenched) and calcium-unsaturated (unquenched) condition, overcoming the issue of lack of internal concentration standards.
source: Two-fluorophore genetically encoded calcium indicators (GECI) relying on Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) can take on a calcium-saturated (quenched) and calcium-unsaturated (unquenched) condition, overcoming this issue.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about FRET-based calcium indicators.

claim: Intravital application of quantitative FRET has been hampered by light distortion effects in deeper tissue.
source: However, intravital application of quantitative FRET has been hampered by light distortion effects in deeper tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations in the field.

claim: Differential scattering and photobleaching properties of the two fluorophores would lead to a false bias towards a higher quenching state.
source: The differential scattering and photobleaching properties of the two fluorophores would lead to a false bias towards a higher quenching state.
evidence: This is an inference about technical artifacts in FRET imaging.

claim: A single-cell fluorescence lifetime imaging approach for absolute calcium quantification in living organisms is tissue depth-independent.
source: We here introduce a single-cell fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) approach for absolute calcium quantification in living organisms that is tissue depth-independent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing consistent measurements at different tissue depths.

claim: FLIM technologies have been employed in the past 30 years to sense changes in pH, ionic strength, pO2, metabolism, and many other cellular parameters within living cells.
source: Both time-domain and frequency-domain FLIM technologies have been employed in the past 30 years to sense changes in pH, ionic strength, pO2, metabolism, and many other cellular parameters within living cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FLIM applications.

claim: The impact of cellular parameters on chemical structure can change the fluorescence lifetime of analyzed fluorophores (Elson et al., 2004; Lakowicz et al., 1992; Le Marois and Suhling, 2017).
source: Due to the impact of these parameters on the chemical structure, the fluorescence lifetime of the analyzed fluorophores can change (Elson et al., 2004; Lakowicz et al., 1992; Le Marois and Suhling, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The versatility of FLIM to quantify FRET quenching has been demonstrated and applied in various biological contexts (Chen et al., 2003; Levitt et al., 2020; Mossakowski et al., 2015).
source: Particularly, the versatility of FLIM to quantify FRET quenching has been demonstrated and applied in various biological contexts (Chen et al., 2003; Levitt et al., 2020; Mossakowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TN-XXL is able to measure fluctuations in cytoplasmic calcium concentration through the calcium binding property of the muscle protein troponin C (Mank et al., 2006).
source: The enhanced cyan fluorescent protein (eCFP)/citrine-FRET pair-GECI TN-XXL is able to measure fluctuations in cytoplasmic calcium concentration through the calcium binding property of the muscle protein troponin C (TnC) (Mank et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mank et al., 2006.

claim: Calcium binding to the fluorophore-linker TnC quenches eCFP fluorescence through energy transfer to citrine (FRET), linking decreasing eCFP fluorescence lifetime to increasing calcium concentration.
source: Calcium binding to the fluorophore-linker TnC quenches eCFP fluorescence through energy transfer to citrine (FRET), linking decreasing eCFP fluorescence lifetime to increasing calcium concentration.
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of FRET-based calcium indicators.

claim: eCFP fluorescence lifetime changes with refractive index (Strickler and Berg, 1962) and may change upon large shifts in pH value, ionic strength, oxygenation, or temperature.
source: Whereas eCFP fluorescence lifetime changes with refractive index (Strickler and Berg, 1962) and may change upon large shifts in pH value, ionic strength, oxygenation, or temperature, these parameters hardly vary in the cytosol of living cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and established knowledge about fluorophore properties.

claim: pH value, ionic strength, oxygenation, and temperature hardly vary in the cytosol of living cells.
source: Whereas eCFP fluorescence lifetime changes with refractive index (Strickler and Berg, 1962) and may change upon large shifts in pH value, ionic strength, oxygenation, or temperature, these parameters hardly vary in the cytosol of living cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cellular physiology.

claim: Only changes in cytosolic calcium concentration are expected to have an impact on the fluorescence lifetime of eCFP as donor in the TN-XXL construct.
source: Thus, we expect only changes in cytosolic calcium concentration to have an impact on the fluorescence lifetime of eCFP as donor in the TN-XXL construct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability of other cellular parameters.

claim: Phasor analysis of FLIM data elegantly condenses multicomponent fluorescent decay curves into single vector-based information (Digman et al., 2008).
source: In addition, phasor analysis of FLIM data elegantly condenses multicomponent fluorescent decay curves into single vector-based information (the phasor) (Digman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Digman et al., 2008.

claim: The titration curve of TN-XXL by Geiger et al. was confirmed in the experimental setup (Geiger et al., 2012).
source: For calcium concentration analysis in microscopic images, we first took advantage of the previously published titration curve of TN-XXL by Geiger et al., which we also confirmed in our experimental setup (Geiger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation.

claim: The phasor-based calibration strategy to quantify calcium levels in vivo proposed by Celli and colleagues was adapted to the TN-XXL construct expressed in B lymphocytes (Celli et al., 2010).
source: We further adapted the phasor-based calibration strategy to quantify calcium levels in vivo proposed by Celli and colleagues to the TN-XXL construct expressed in B lymphocytes (Celli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the methodology described and a citation.

claim: Short- and long-term changes in absolute calcium concentrations within B cells during affinity maturation and differentiation into antibody-producing plasma cells can be described using the developed method.
source: With this method, we are able to describe short- and long-term changes in absolute calcium concentrations within B cells during affinity maturation and differentiation into antibody-producing plasma cells.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: YellowCaB mice express cytosolic TN-XXL in all CD19-positive cells.
source: We here describe the calcium reporter mouse strain 'YellowCaB' (termed after energy transfer to the yellow fluorescent protein citrine in case of calcium present in the cytosol of B cells). These mice express cytosolic TN-XXL in all CD19-positive cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing TN-XXL expression in CD19+ cells.

claim: Intravital FLIM of adoptively transferred YellowCaB cells shows that calcium concentrations are highly dynamic in B cells involved in the GC reaction.
source: Intravital FLIM of adoptively transferred YellowCaB cells shows that calcium concentrations are highly dynamic in B cells involved in the GC reaction.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved imaging data.

claim: Different patterns of calcium fluctuation regarding amplitude and baseline exist within non-activated and AG experienced cells and plasma blasts.
source: We describe different patterns of calcium fluctuation regarding amplitude and baseline within non-activated and AG experienced cells and plasma blasts.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of calcium dynamics in different B cell subsets.

claim: Ca2+-high differentiated B cells and plasma blast populations emerge, which might point to cells undergoing metabolic stress.
source: We observe the emergence of Ca2+-high differentiated B cells and plasma blast populations, which might point to cells undergoing metabolic stress.
evidence: This is based on data showing high calcium populations and speculation about their metabolic state.

claim: Mice expressing a loxP-flanked STOP sequence followed by the TN-XXL-construct inserted into the ROSA26 locus were crossed with the CD19-Cre strain (Rickert et al., 1997).
source: Mice expressing a loxP-flanked STOP sequence followed by the TN-XXL-construct inserted into the ROSA26 locus were crossed with the CD19-Cre strain (Rickert et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for generating YellowCaB mice.

claim: The offspring had exclusive expression of the GECI TN-XXL in CD19+ B lymphocytes.
source: The offspring had exclusive expression of the GECI TN-XXL in CD19+ B lymphocytes, as confirmed by visualization of eCFP and citrine fluorescence by confocal microscopy after magnetic B cell isolation (Figure 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1a, b.

claim: YellowCaB cells excited with a 405 nm laser show yellow emission attributable to baseline FRET representing steady-state calcium levels.
source: These YellowCaB cells were excited with a 405 nm laser that is capable of exciting eCFP but not citrine. The detection of yellow emission thus can be attributed to baseline FRET representing steady-state calcium levels.
evidence: This is based on the spectral properties of the fluorophores and FRET mechanism.

claim: Citrine was found to be present in a substantial part of CD19+ B lymphocytes and was not detectable in the CD19- population (Figure 1c).
source: Citrine was found to be present in a substantial part of CD19+ B lymphocytes and was not detectable in the CD19- population (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Cd19cre/+ mice heterozygous for TN-XXL and Cd19cre/+ mice homozygous for TN-XXL did not differ in the proportion of cells within the CD19+GFP+ population.
source: Cd19cre/+ mice heterozygous for TN-XXL and Cd19cre/+ mice homozygous for TN-XXL did not differ in the proportion of cells within the CD19+GFP+ population, nor did male and female mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Male and female YellowCaB mice did not differ in the proportion of cells within the CD19+GFP+ population.
source: Cd19cre/+ mice heterozygous for TN-XXL and Cd19cre/+ mice homozygous for TN-XXL did not differ in the proportion of cells within the CD19+GFP+ population, nor did male and female mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No differences in total cell numbers and B cell numbers between Cd19cre/+Tn-xxl+/-, Cd19cre/+ Tn-xxl+/+, and wild-type mice were detected.
source: In addition, no differences in total cell numbers and B cell numbers between Cd19cre/+Tn-xxl+/-, Cd19cre/+ Tn-xxl+/+, and wild-type mice were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When stimulated with ionomycin, a steep increase of the FRET level over baseline was recorded by flow cytometry in YellowCaB cells.
source: When stimulated with ionomycin, a steep increase of the FRET level over baseline was recorded by flow cytometry in the GFP-channel after excitation with the 405 nm laser.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing FRET increase after ionomycin stimulation.

claim: Calcium-dependence of the signal increase was independently confirmed by staining with the calcium sensitive dye X-Rhod-1 (Figure 1d; Li et al., 2003).
source: Calcium-dependence of the signal increase was further independently confirmed by staining with the calcium sensitive dye X-Rhod-1, that shows a red fluorescence signal increase after calcium binding (Figure 1d; Li et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by X-Rhod-1 staining data shown in Figure 1d and a citation.

claim: A decrease of the eCFP signal concurrent with an increased citrine fluorescence was detected after the addition of 4 µg/ml ionomycin to continuous flow of 6 mM Krebs–Ringer solution.
source: As expected, we detected a decrease of the eCFP signal, concurrent with an increased citrine fluorescence after the addition of 4 µg/ml ionomycin to continuous flow of 6 mM Krebs–Ringer solution.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data.

claim: Ionomycin treatment resulted in a maximal elevation of ΔR/R of 50–55% over baseline (Figure 1f).
source: Overall, this resulted in a maximal elevation of ΔR/R of 50–55% over baseline (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by FRET ratio measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: In approximately three quarters of the cells, FRET in response to ionomycin treatment was detectable.
source: Analysis of >100 cells showed that approximately in three quarters of the cells we were able to detect FRET in response to ionomycin treatment, and that the majority of these cells showed 35–40% FRET signal change.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of >100 cells shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The majority of cells responding to ionomycin showed 35–40% FRET signal change.
source: Analysis of >100 cells showed that approximately in three quarters of the cells we were able to detect FRET in response to ionomycin treatment, and that the majority of these cells showed 35–40% FRET signal change.
evidence: This is supported by histogram analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: A change of 20% ΔR/R was defined as a relevant threshold for the positive evaluation of responsiveness.
source: According to the two populations visible in the histogram, we defined a change of 20% ΔR/R as a relevant threshold for the positive evaluation of responsiveness (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is based on the distribution of responses shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Functional and well-tolerated expression of TN-XXL exclusively in murine CD19+ B cells for measurement of changes of cytoplasmic calcium concentrations was achieved.
source: In conclusion, we achieved the functional and well-tolerated expression of TN-XXL exclusively in murine CD19+ B cells for measurement of changes of cytoplasmic calcium concentrations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the data presented in the Results section.

claim: Stimulation of isolated YellowCaB cells with 10 µg/ml anti-IgM F(ab)2 fragments induced an elevated FRET signal with a peak height of >30% that lasted over 3 min (Figure 2a).
source: To test the functional performance of the GECI TN-XXL in YellowCaB cells, we stimulated isolated YellowCaB cells with 10 µg/ml anti-IgM F(ab)2 fragments to activate the BCR. In an open culture imaging chamber, we induced an elevated FRET signal with a peak height of >30% that lasted over 3 min (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The FRET signal declines after 3 min, probably due to BCR internalization or the activity of ion pumps.
source: The signal declines after this time span, probably due to BCR internalization or the activity of ion pumps.
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms of BCR signaling regulation.

claim: An antibody concentration of 2 µg/ml was not enough to provoke calcium flux.
source: We tested antibody concentrations at 2, 4, 10, and 20 µg/ml. An antibody concentration of 2 µg/ml was not enough to provoke calcium flux (data not shown), whereas at 4 µg/ml anti-IgM-F(ab)2 we observed 20% an elevated ΔR/R over baseline (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of different antibody concentrations.

claim: At 4 µg/ml anti-IgM-F(ab)2, 20% elevated ΔR/R over baseline was observed (Figure 2b).
source: We tested antibody concentrations at 2, 4, 10, and 20 µg/ml. An antibody concentration of 2 µg/ml was not enough to provoke calcium flux (data not shown), whereas at 4 µg/ml anti-IgM-F(ab)2 we observed 20% an elevated ΔR/R over baseline (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: At 20 µg/ml anti-IgM-F(ab)2, no further FRET increase was detected.
source: At 20 µg/ml anti-IgM-F(ab)2, we detected no further FRET increase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: A concentration dependency of the GECI TN-XXL exists with saturating conditions at 10 µg/ml BCR heavy chain stimulation.
source: Thus, we conclude a concentration dependency of the GECI TN-XXL and saturating conditions at 10 µg/ml BCR heavy chain stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response data.

claim: A residual FRET signal of about 7% compared to baseline values was measured for approximately 3.5 additional minutes after the initial FRET signal declined (Figure 2a).
source: Interestingly, the reaction is not completely cut off after the FRET signal has declined, but a residual FRET signal of about 7% compared to baseline values was measured for approximately 3.5 additional minutes (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 2a.

claim: B cells seem to be able to store extra calcium within the cytoplasm for some time.
source: Thus, B cells seem to be able to store extra calcium within the cytoplasm for some time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of sustained elevated calcium after stimulation.

claim: It is possible to stimulate YellowCaB cells more than once under continuous perfusion with Ringer solution.
source: We therefore wondered if it is possible to stimulate YellowCaB cells more than once. For this purpose, we connected our imaging culture chamber to a peristaltic pump and took advantage of the fact that under continuous perfusion with Ringer solution the flow will dilute the antibody out of the chamber. This way, it is possible to stimulate B cells several times rapidly and subsequently, before BCRs are internalized, indicated by multiple peaks in ΔR/R (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by repeated stimulation experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Stimulation of the BCR light chain using an anti-kappa antibody led to calcium increase within YellowCaB cells.
source: In addition, stimulation of the BCR light chain using an anti-kappa antibody led to calcium increase within YellowCaB cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The FRET peak resulting from anti-kappa antibody stimulation is shaped differently, and concentrations > 150 µg/ml antibody were needed to generate a response.
source: Of note, the resulting FRET peak is shaped differently, and concentrations > 150 µg/ml antibody were needed in order to generate a response.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of anti-kappa stimulation.

claim: T cell engagement and the binding of microbial targets to innate receptors like TLRs have been described to raise cytoplasmic calcium in B cells (Ojaniemi et al., 2003; Pone et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2014).
source: Since T cell engagement and the binding of microbial targets to innate receptors like TLRs have also been described to raise cytoplasmic calcium in B cells (Ojaniemi et al., 2003; Pone et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2014), we investigated the response of YellowCaB cells after incubation with anti-CD40 antibodies, as well as the TLR4 and TLR9 stimuli lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and cytosine-phosphate-guanine-rich regions of bacterial DNA (CpG), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: No reaction to anti-CD40 treatment alone was detected within the same cells.
source: Within the same cells, we detected no reaction to anti-CD40 treatment alone, but observed three types of shapes in post-CD40 BCR-stimulated calcium responses, which differed from anti-CD40-untreated cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of CD40 stimulation.

claim: Three types of shapes in post-CD40 BCR-stimulated calcium responses were observed: sustained, transient, or intermediate (Figure 2c).
source: These calcium flux patterns were either sustained, transient, or of an intermediate shape (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Sustained calcium flux saturated the sensor at a level comparable to that achieved by ionomycin treatment.
source: Sustained calcium flux even saturated the sensor at a level comparable to that achieved by ionomycin treatment.
evidence: This is based on comparison of FRET levels between sustained flux and ionomycin treatment.

claim: Cells that showed only intermediate flux maintained their ability to respond to ionomycin treatment at high FRET levels (Figure 2c).
source: Cells that showed only intermediate flux maintained their ability to respond to ionomycin treatment at high FRET levels, as demonstrated by the ΔR/R reaching 0.4 again after stimulation (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by sequential stimulation data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Integrated TLR and BCR stimulation affected the appearance of the calcium signal.
source: Furthermore, integrated TLR and BCR stimulation affected the appearance of the calcium signal.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of combined TLR and BCR stimulation.

claim: The addition of TLR9 stimulus CpG alone had no effect on YellowCaB FRET levels.
source: The addition of TLR9 stimulus CpG alone had no effect on YellowCaB FRET levels; however, the subsequent FRET peak in response to anti-Ig-F(ab)2 was delayed (Figure 2d, e).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 2d, e.

claim: The subsequent FRET peak in response to anti-Ig-F(ab)2 was delayed after CpG treatment (Figure 2d, e).
source: The addition of TLR9 stimulus CpG alone had no effect on YellowCaB FRET levels; however, the subsequent FRET peak in response to anti-Ig-F(ab)2 was delayed (Figure 2d, e).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 2d, e.

claim: TLR4 stimulation via LPS could elevate calcium concentration of B cells, but only to a minor extent (Figure 2e).
source: TLR4 stimulation via LPS could elevate calcium concentration of B cells, but only to a minor extent (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 2e.

claim: When TLR4 stimulation by LPS was performed before BCR stimulation, decreased FRET levels in response to anti-IgM-F(ab)2 were observed.
source: When TLR4 stimulation by LPS was performed before BCR stimulation, decreased FRET levels in response to anti-IgM-F(ab)2 were observed.
evidence: This is supported by sequential stimulation experiments.

claim: B cells are able to collect and integrate multiple BCR-induced calcium signals in order to become fully activated.
source: We conclude that, in order to become fully activated, B cells are able to collect and integrate multiple BCR-induced calcium signals and that signaling patterns are further shaped by innate signals or T cell help.
evidence: This is inferred from the repeated stimulation experiments.

claim: Signaling patterns are further shaped by innate signals or T cell help.
source: We conclude that, in order to become fully activated, B cells are able to collect and integrate multiple BCR-induced calcium signals and that signaling patterns are further shaped by innate signals or T cell help.
evidence: This is inferred from the TLR and CD40 stimulation experiments.

claim: BCR inhibition abolishes a FRET signal change in response to anti-IgM-F(ab)2.
source: BCR inhibition abolishes a FRET signal change in response to anti-IgM-F(ab)2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: No FRET peak was detected after applying CXCL12 in vitro, probably because of lacking GECI sensitivity to small cytoplasmic changes.
source: Of note, we excluded the possibility that measured signal changes were related to chemokine stimulation. In vitro, we detected no FRET peak after applying CXCL12, probably because of lacking GECI sensitivity to small cytoplasmic changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of CXCL12 stimulation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, d.

claim: The YellowCaB system is well suited for the detection of BCR-induced cytosolic calcium concentration changes.
source: Thus, the YellowCaB system is well suited for the detection of BCR-induced cytosolic calcium concentration changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental validation of the system.

claim: Activated TN-XXL+ YellowCaB cells migrated into the GC, as confirmed by positive PNA- and anti-FP-immunofluorescence histology (Figure 3a).
source: Activated TN-XXL+ YellowCaB cells had migrated into the GC, as confirmed by positive PNA- and anti-FP-immunofluorescence histology (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The movement of single YellowCaB cells is traceable in vivo.
source: Our experiments revealed that the movement of single YellowCaB cells is traceable in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by intravital imaging experiments.

claim: Calcium fluctuations can be made visible by intensity changes in an extra channel that depicts the FRET signal.
source: Calcium fluctuations can be made visible by intensity changes in an extra channel that depicts the FRET signal, as calculated from relative quenching of TN-XXL.
evidence: This is based on the imaging methodology described.

claim: A sustained increase in FRET signal was observed after prolonged contacts between two YellowCaB cells (Figure 3b, Video 1).
source: Color coding of intensity changes in the FRET channel showed time-dependent fluctuations of the signal and, in some particular cases, a sustained increase after prolonged contacts between two YellowCaB cells (Figure 3b, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3b and Video 1.

claim: FRET intensity seemed to be mostly fluctuating around low levels in moving cells, whereas sustained increase required cell arrest (Negulescu et al., 1996; Shulman et al., 2014).
source: Interestingly, FRET intensity seemed to be mostly fluctuating around low levels in moving cells, whereas sustained increase required cell arrest, as reported previously (Negulescu et al., 1996; Shulman et al., 2014), (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: The threshold for a strong and sustained colocalization of FDCs and B cells was set to an intensity of 150 AU within the colocalization channel.
source: We set the threshold for a strong and sustained colocalization of FDCs and B cells to an intensity of 150 AU within the colocalization channel. At this value, the decay of the biexponential fit was below 10%.
evidence: This is based on analysis of colocalization intensity distribution shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Several transient B-cell–FDC contacts in cell 1 were followed by a gradual increase of ΔR/R, indicating an increase of cytoplasmic calcium concentration (Figure 3d).
source: We detected several transient B-cell–FDC contacts in cell 1 that were followed by a gradual increase of ΔR/R, indicating an increase of cytoplasmic calcium concentration (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Cell 2 kept strong FDC contact over the whole imaging time and maintained elevated, mostly stable values.
